```{python}
#| include: false

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

from palmerpenguins import load_penguins

from plotnine import (
    ggplot, aes, geom_col, geom_boxplot, geom_jitter,
    geom_tile, geom_text, labs, theme_minimal, theme,
    scale_fill_manual, scale_fill_gradient2,
    element_text
)

from scipy.stats import kruskal, chi2_contingency
from IPython.display import display, HTML

# Load data
penguins = load_penguins()

clean = penguins.dropna(
    subset=["species", "island"]
).copy()

body_mass_data = clean.dropna(
    subset=["body_mass_g"]
).copy()

# Blue color palette
species_colors = {
    "Adelie": "#173F73",
    "Chinstrap": "#438CCB",
    "Gentoo": "#91C9F2"
}

island_colors = {
    "Biscoe": "#173F73",
    "Dream": "#438CCB",
    "Torgersen": "#91C9F2"
}

# Summary values
total_penguins = len(clean)
total_species = clean["species"].nunique()
total_islands = clean["island"].nunique()
average_body_mass = body_mass_data["body_mass_g"].mean()

# Species counts
species_counts = (
    clean["species"]
    .value_counts()
    .rename_axis("species")
    .reset_index(name="count")
)

# Island counts
island_counts = (
    clean["island"]
    .value_counts()
    .rename_axis("island")
    .reset_index(name="count")
)

# Species by island
species_island_counts = (
    clean.groupby(["island", "species"])
    .size()
    .reset_index(name="count")
)

# Descriptive statistics by species
descriptive_stats = (
    body_mass_data.groupby("species")["body_mass_g"]
    .agg(
        Count="count",
        Mean="mean",
        Median="median",
        SD="std",
        Minimum="min",
        Maximum="max"
    )
    .round(2)
    .reset_index()
)

# Overall body mass statistics
overall_stats = body_mass_data["body_mass_g"].agg(
    ["count", "mean", "median", "std", "min", "max"]
).round(2)

# Kruskal-Wallis test
species_order = ["Adelie", "Chinstrap", "Gentoo"]

body_mass_groups = [
    body_mass_data.loc[
        body_mass_data["species"] == species,
        "body_mass_g"
    ].values
    for species in species_order
]

kruskal_result = kruskal(*body_mass_groups)

kruskal_h = kruskal_result.statistic
kruskal_p = kruskal_result.pvalue

number_of_groups = len(body_mass_groups)
body_mass_sample_size = sum(len(group) for group in body_mass_groups)

epsilon_squared = max(
    0,
    (kruskal_h - number_of_groups + 1) /
    (body_mass_sample_size - number_of_groups)
)

# Chi-square test
contingency_table = pd.crosstab(
    clean["species"],
    clean["island"]
)

chi2, chi2_p, degrees_freedom, expected = chi2_contingency(
    contingency_table
)

sample_size = contingency_table.to_numpy().sum()

minimum_dimension = min(
    contingency_table.shape[0] - 1,
    contingency_table.shape[1] - 1
)

cramers_v = np.sqrt(
    chi2 / (sample_size * minimum_dimension)
)

# Expected frequencies and Pearson residuals
expected_table = pd.DataFrame(
    expected,
    index=contingency_table.index,
    columns=contingency_table.columns
)

minimum_expected = expected.min()

pearson_residuals = (
    contingency_table - expected_table
) / np.sqrt(expected_table)

residual_data = (
    pearson_residuals
    .reset_index()
    .melt(
        id_vars="species",
        var_name="island",
        value_name="residual"
    )
)

observed_data = (
    contingency_table
    .reset_index()
    .melt(
        id_vars="species",
        var_name="island",
        value_name="observed"
    )
)

residual_data = residual_data.merge(
    observed_data,
    on=["species", "island"]
)

residual_data["label"] = residual_data.apply(
    lambda row: (
        f'{int(row["observed"])}'
        f'\n({row["residual"]:+.1f})'
    ),
    axis=1
)
```

## Row: Penguin Distribution {height="380px"}

```{python}
#| title: "Penguin Observations by Species"

species_plot = (
    ggplot(
        species_counts,
        aes(x="species", y="count", fill="species")
    )
    + geom_col(width=0.65)
    + scale_fill_manual(values=species_colors)
    + labs(
        title="Penguins by Species",
        x="Species",
        y="Observations"
    )
    + theme_minimal()
    + theme(
        legend_position="none",
        figure_size=(7, 4)
    )
)

species_plot
```

Adelie penguins have the highest number of observations, followed by Gentoo and Chinstrap. This makes Adelie the most frequently represented species in the dataset.

```{python}
#| title: "Penguin Observations by Island"

island_plot = (
    ggplot(
        island_counts,
        aes(x="island", y="count", fill="island")
    )
    + geom_col(width=0.65)
    + scale_fill_manual(values=island_colors)
    + labs(
        title="Penguins by Island",
        x="Island",
        y="Observations"
    )
    + theme_minimal()
    + theme(
        legend_position="none",
        figure_size=(7, 4)
    )
)

island_plot
```

Biscoe Island has the highest number of recorded penguins, followed by Dream and Torgersen. This shows that Biscoe has the greatest representation in the dataset.

```{python}
#| title: "Species Distribution Across Islands"

island_species_plot = (
    ggplot(
        species_island_counts,
        aes(x="island", y="count", fill="species")
    )
    + geom_col()
    + scale_fill_manual(values=species_colors)
    + labs(
        title="Species Across Islands",
        x="Island",
        y="Penguins",
        fill="Species"
    )
    + theme_minimal()
    + theme(
        figure_size=(7, 4),
        legend_position="bottom"
    )
)

island_species_plot
```

Adelie penguins are recorded on all three islands, while Gentoo penguins appear only on Biscoe and Chinstrap penguins only on Dream. This demonstrates differences in species representation across the islands.

```{python}
#| title: "Body Mass Summary by Species"

display(
```

The table summarizes the count, mean, median, standard deviation, minimum, and maximum body mass for each species. These metrics describe typical body mass and variation within each group.

```{python}
})

display(overall_table.style.hide(axis="index"))
```

The overall statistics describe body mass across all penguins with available measurements. The mean and median show the center of the data, while the standard deviation and range show its variability.

## Row: Inferential Statistics - Kruskal-Wallis {height="520px"}

```{python}
#| title: "Body Mass Differences by Species"

body_mass_plot = (
    ggplot(
        body_mass_data,
        aes(
            x="species",
            y="body_mass_g",
            fill="species"
        )
    )
    + geom_boxplot(alpha=0.85, width=0.6)
    + geom_jitter(
        width=0.12,
        alpha=0.25,
        size=1.5,
        color="#173F73"
    )
    + scale_fill_manual(values=species_colors)
    + labs(
        title="Body Mass by Species",
        subtitle="Kruskal-Wallis comparison",
        x="Penguin Species",
        y="Body Mass (g)"
    )
    + theme_minimal()
    + theme(
        legend_position="none",
        figure_size=(9, 5),
        axis_title=element_text(size=12),
        axis_text=element_text(size=11),
        plot_title=element_text(size=16, weight="bold"),
        plot_subtitle=element_text(size=11)
    )
)

body_mass_plot
```

```{python}
#| title: "Kruskal-Wallis Statistical Results"

kruskal_summary = pd.DataFrame({
    "Metric": [
        "H-statistic",
        "P-value",
        "Epsilon-squared",
        "Significance level"
    ],
    "Result": [
        f"{kruskal_h:.4f}",
        f"{kruskal_p:.6g}",
        f"{epsilon_squared:.4f}",
        "0.05"
    ]
})

display(kruskal_summary.style.hide(axis="index"))
```

**Interpretation**

The Kruskal-Wallis test examines whether body mass distributions differ among Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo penguins. A p-value below 0.05 indicates evidence of a difference among at least two species. The test does not identify exactly which species differ.

## Row: Inferential Statistics - Chi-Square {height="520px"}

```{python}
#| title: "Association Between Species and Island"

chi_square_plot = (
    ggplot(
        residual_data,
        aes(
            x="island",
            y="species",
            fill="residual"
        )
    )
    + geom_tile(color="white")
    + geom_text(
        aes(label="label"),
        size=9,
        color="#173F73"
    )
    + scale_fill_gradient2(
        low="#91C9F2",
        mid="#FFFFFF",
        high="#173F73",
        midpoint=0
    )
    + labs(
        title="Species and Island Association",
        subtitle="Observed counts and Pearson residuals",
        x="Island",
        y="Penguin Species",
        fill="Pearson Residual"
    )
    + theme_minimal()
    + theme(
        figure_size=(9, 5),
        axis_title=element_text(size=12),
        axis_text=element_text(size=11),
        plot_title=element_text(size=16, weight="bold"),
        plot_subtitle=element_text(size=11),
        legend_title=element_text(size=11),
        legend_text=element_text(size=10)
    )
)

chi_square_plot
```

```{python}
#| title: "Chi-Square Statistical Results"

chi_square_summary = pd.DataFrame({
    "Metric": [
        "Chi-square statistic",
        "Degrees of freedom",
        "P-value",
        "Cramer's V",
        "Minimum expected cell count",
        "Significance level"
    ],
    "Result": [
        f"{chi2:.4f}",
        str(degrees_freedom),
        f"{chi2_p:.6g}",
        f"{cramers_v:.4f}",
        f"{minimum_expected:.2f}",
        "0.05"
    ]
})

display(chi_square_summary.style.hide(axis="index"))
```

**Interpretation**

The chi-square test examines whether penguin species and island are associated. A p-value below 0.05 indicates evidence of an association. Positive Pearson residuals indicate more observations than expected, while negative residuals indicate fewer.

**Assumption Check:** The minimum expected cell count is displayed in the statistical results. The usual chi-square approximation is generally considered appropriate when expected cell counts are sufficiently large.

## Row: Overall Conclusion {height="150px"}

The Palmer Penguins dataset shows differences in species frequency, island distribution, and body mass. Descriptive statistics summarize these patterns, while inferential tests examine differences in body mass and associations between species and island. These findings describe the available dataset and do not establish causation.
